issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'fire or flames' is hard to reconcile as a salient trauma trigger unless there is specific additional context linking the illness to fire; this trigger appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking doors and windows being locked implies a home-intrusion/external attack danger theme, which does not fit well with the illness-related threat pattern suggested by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: Avoiding attention to one's own body is coherent for illness trauma, but it does not fit well with the selected threat theme of locking/checking doors and windows; together these items suggest incompatible danger models (internal bodily threat vs external intruder threat).

vignette: At 54 years old, Lila found herself reflecting on the harrowing experience that had irreversibly altered the trajectory of her life. Several years ago, she was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness that led to an extended hospital stay. The sterile antiseptic smell of the hospital still haunted her; it was a scent that triggered visceral memories, rushing back with the intensity of a tidal wave. The heavy breathing of the medical staff during her treatments echoed in her mind, a reminder of her own labored breaths as she fought for her life. Each anniversary of that fateful day gripped her with dread, leaving her unable to shake the feelings of vulnerability and fear that resurfaced each year, as if time itself conspired to remind her of her fragility. In the wake of her trauma, Lila developed a habit of dissociation, often pretending that the illness had happened to someone else. This strategy allowed her to create a psychological distance from the pain, yet it also led her to feel isolated, as if she were an observer in her own life. She often found herself engulfed in counterfactual thinking, imagining how her life might have unfolded differently had the illness not struck. When the weight of those thoughts became unbearable, she would retreat into her dissociative habits, believing that ignoring her feelings was the only way to manage the overwhelming anxiety that surged with every reminder of her past. These thoughts would spiral out of control, leaving her stuck in a loop of despair about what could have been. In her daily life as an electrician, she meticulously avoided anything that reminded her of the medical world; she shunned hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations, convinced that any encounter with these settings would plunge her back into the depths of her trauma. Each time she encountered a trigger, whether it was the sight of an ambulance or the sound of medical jargon, she would retreat further into her dissociative habits, convincing herself that avoiding these reminders was the only way to stave off the overwhelming anxiety that threatened to consume her. Lila's body remained on high alert, a constant state of tension that she could neither understand nor control. Each time she caught the faintest whiff of antiseptic or overheard a heavy breath, her heart would race, her muscles tightening as if preparing for an imminent threat. It was as if her body had learned to react before her mind could catch up, leaving her grappling with overwhelming physical sensations that felt foreign and frightening. This hyper-arousal only reinforced her maladaptive strategies, as she sought to retreat further into her dissociative habits to escape the distressing reality of her own body. Each time she was confronted with a trigger, such as the antiseptic smell or the sounds of medical equipment, she would immediately retreat into her dissociative state, believing it was the only way to cope with the overwhelming anxiety. However, this retreat only reinforced her triggers, as every avoidance created a new association in her mind, mapping out areas of her life she felt she could no longer navigate without fear. Her reliance on these strategies ultimately increased her perception of threat; without ever challenging her fears, she felt the danger of her past experiences lurking just beneath the surface, as if she had never truly escaped. The interplay between her triggers and her maladaptive responses became a vicious cycle. The more she avoided reminders of her illness, the more her anxiety thrived in the shadows, amplifying her physical reactivity. Each time she steered clear of a hospital or a medical discussion, the threat to her emotional well-being felt more pronounced, heightening her sense of danger and vulnerability. This sense of threat made her convinced that her only option was to avoid situations where she might feel vulnerable, leading her to withdraw from social gatherings and even change her routes to work to steer clear of any reminders. "However, this withdrawal created new triggers; every time she missed a gathering or skipped a check-up, it reinforced her belief that the world outside her carefully constructed bubble was fraught with peril." Lila's attempts to shield herself from the realities of her experience inadvertently kept her trapped within its clutches, as her avoidance reinforced the very fears she was trying to escape. By avoiding situations that reminded her of her illness, she never allowed herself to experience the safety of those environments, which left her convinced that danger was still lurking around every corner. Without ever testing her fears, she remained trapped in a cycle where her avoidance preserved the very threat she sought to escape, as her nervous system still responded to the past as though it were an ongoing reality. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing." "With that level of threat always looming, she found herself planning exits from social situations and avoiding eye contact, as if any connection could pull her back into danger." This ongoing struggle culminated in a moment of clarity during a routine day at work. "When the threat felt this close, she stopped taking that route to work entirely - better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again." Lila found herself on a job site, surrounded by the familiar sounds of tools and machinery, when the unmistakable scent of antiseptic wafted through the air. "Yet, never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed - the threat remained as high as the day it was set." Immediately, her breath hitched, and her heart raced, a physical manifestation of the unrelenting fear that gripped her. It was a moment that forced her to confront the toll her trauma had taken on her life - her relationships suffered, her work became a challenge, and she often felt detached from those around her. Realizing she could no longer navigate this labyrinth of fear alone, Lila made the difficult decision to seek help. What frightened her most was the thought of being unable to reclaim her life, while what she hoped for was to find a way to live fully again, free from the shadows of her past. "Each time she passed a hospital or saw an ambulance, that initial jolt of fear would send her mind racing, and she would quickly divert her route, believing that avoiding these places was the only way to keep her anxiety at bay." "However, her safety behaviors had drawn a map of the event around her: everywhere she kept at arm's length became its own new reminder, reinforcing the very fears she was trying to escape."

Without ever testing her fears, she remained trapped in a cycle where her avoidance preserved the very threat she sought to escape, as her nervous system still responded to the past as though it were an ongoing reality. This ongoing struggle culminated in a moment of clarity during a routine day at work. Immediately, her breath hitched, and her heart raced, a physical manifestation of the unrelenting fear that gripped her. Realizing she could no longer navigate this labyrinth of fear alone, Lila made the difficult decision to seek help. The sterile antiseptic smell of the hospital still haunted her; it was a scent that triggered visceral memories, rushing back with the intensity of a tidal wave. The heavy breathing of the medical staff during her treatments echoed in her mind, a reminder of her own labored breaths as she fought for her life. Each anniversary of that fateful day gripped her with dread, leaving her unable to shake the feelings of vulnerability and fear that resurfaced each year, as if time itself conspired to remind her of her fragility. In the wake of her trauma, Lila developed a habit of dissociation, often pretending that the illness had happened to someone else. This strategy allowed her to create a psychological distance from the pain, yet it also led her to feel isolated, as if she were an observer in her own life. She often found herself engulfed in counterfactual thinking, imagining how her life might have unfolded differently had the illness not struck. When the weight of those thoughts became unbearable, she would retreat into her dissociative habits, believing that ignoring her feelings was the only way to manage the overwhelming anxiety that surged with every reminder of her past. These thoughts would spiral out of control, leaving her stuck in a loop of despair about what could have been. In her daily life as an electrician, she meticulously avoided anything that reminded her of the medical world; she shunned hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations, convinced that any encounter with these settings would plunge her back into the depths of her trauma. Each time she encountered a trigger, whether it was the sight of an ambulance or the sound of medical jargon, she would retreat further into her dissociative habits, convincing herself that avoiding these reminders was the only way to stave off the overwhelming anxiety that threatened to consume her. Lila's body remained on high alert, a constant state of tension that she could neither understand nor control. Each time she caught the faintest whiff of antiseptic or overheard a heavy breath, her heart would race, her muscles tightening as if preparing for an imminent threat. It was as if her body had learned to react before her mind could catch up, leaving her grappling with overwhelming physical sensations that felt foreign and frightening. This hyper-arousal only reinforced her maladaptive strategies, as she sought to retreat further into her dissociative habits to escape the distressing reality of her own body. Each time she was confronted with a trigger, such as the antiseptic smell or the sounds of medical equipment, she would immediately retreat into her dissociative state, believing it was the only way to cope with the overwhelming anxiety. However, this retreat only reinforced her triggers, as every avoidance created a new association in her mind, mapping out areas of her life she felt she could no longer navigate without fear. Her reliance on these strategies ultimately increased her perception of threat; without ever challenging her fears, she felt the danger of her past experiences lurking just beneath the surface, as if she had never truly escaped. The interplay between her triggers and her maladaptive responses became a vicious cycle. Each time she steered clear of a hospital or a medical discussion, the threat to her emotional well-being felt more pronounced, heightening her sense of danger and vulnerability. This sense of threat made her convinced that her only option was to avoid situations where she might feel vulnerable, leading her to withdraw from social gatherings and even change her routes to work to steer clear of any reminders. "However, this withdrawal created new triggers; every time she missed a gathering or skipped a check-up, it reinforced her belief that the world outside her carefully constructed bubble was fraught with peril." Lila’s attempts to shield herself from the realities of her experience inadvertently kept her trapped within its clutches, as her avoidance reinforced the very fears she was trying to escape. By avoiding situations that reminded her of her illness, she never allowed herself to experience the safety of those environments, which left her convinced that danger was still lurking around every corner. Without ever testing her fears, she remained trapped in a cycle where her avoidance preserved the very threat she sought to escape, as her nervous system still responded to the past as though it were an ongoing reality. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing." "With that level of threat always looming, she found herself planning exits from social situations and avoiding eye contact, as if any connection could pull her back into danger." This ongoing struggle culminated in a moment of clarity during a routine day at work. "When the threat felt this close, she stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again." Lila found herself on a job site, surrounded by the familiar sounds of tools and machinery, when the unmistakable scent of antiseptic wafted through the air. "Yet, never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set." Immediately, her breath hitched, and her heart raced, a physical manifestation of the unrelenting fear that gripped her. It was a moment that forced her to confront the toll her trauma had taken on her life — her relationships suffered, her work became a challenge, and she often felt detached from those around her. Realizing she could no longer navigate this labyrinth of fear alone, Lila made the difficult decision to seek help. What frightened her most was the thought of being unable to reclaim her life, while what she hoped for was to find a way to live fully again, free from the shadows of her past. "Each time she passed a hospital or saw an ambulance, that initial jolt of fear would send her mind racing, and she would quickly divert her route, believing that avoiding these places was the only way to keep her anxiety at bay." "However, her safety behaviors had drawn a map of the event around her: everywhere she kept at arm's length became its own new reminder, reinforcing the very fears she was trying to escape."
